statement: A bishop is a chess piece that moves any number of squares diagonally. A bishop starts in a corner square of a board with 7 rows and 9 columns, coloured like a chessboard. Making as many moves as it likes, how many squares of the board can it visit, including its starting square?

choices.misconception: I counted only the squares on the one diagonal through the corner, forgetting that the bishop can change direction.
I halved the 63 squares and rounded down, not noticing that the colour of the corners is the one with the extra square.
I thought every row had 5 squares of the corner's colour, so 7 × 5, but the rows alternate between 5 and 4.
I thought the bishop could reach every square if it made enough moves.

hints: What happens to the colour of the bishop's square on each move?
A diagonal move never changes the colour of the square, so the bishop is stuck on squares of its starting colour. Count those, and check that it can really reach all of them.
In each row of 9 the colours alternate. Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 start with the corner's colour, rows 2, 4 and 6 start with the other colour.

solutions.reliable: A diagonal move always lands on a square of the same colour, so the bishop only ever visits squares of the corner's colour. Rows 1, 3, 5 and 7 start with that colour and contain 5 such squares each; rows 2, 4 and 6 contain 4 each. That is 4 × 5 + 3 × 4 = 32. On a board this size the bishop can zigzag to every square of its colour, so all 32 can be visited. The transferable idea: colour the board so that a move always keeps (or always switches) the colour, then count by colour.
solutions.elegant: The 63 squares split into 32 of one colour and 31 of the other. With an odd number of rows and of columns, all four corners share a colour, and that is the colour with the extra square: 32.

whyOnTest: Colouring arguments test noticing a property that a move can never change, here the colour of the square the bishop stands on.
